subject: maths
title: Measuring: long, heavy, and full
intro: Measuring means finding out how big, how heavy, or how much something is. Which pencil is longer? Which bag is heavier? Which cup holds more? This lesson starts with comparing things, then shows how we use units so everyone gets the same answer.

sections.heading: Comparing without numbers
body: Before we use numbers, we can just **compare** two things. For length we ask which is **longer** or **shorter**. For weight, which is **heavier** or **lighter**. For how much a container holds (capacity), which is **fuller** or holds **more**. To compare lengths fairly, line the two things up at the same starting point and see which one sticks out further.
In the picture, the pencil bar is longer than the crayon bar, so the pencil is longer.

diagram.caption: Line them up at the same start — the pencil is longer than the crayon.

sections.heading: Measuring with units
body: Saying 'longer' is useful, but to say **how much** longer we need **units** — equal-sized things we count. You could measure a desk in paperclips or hand-spans: 'the desk is 8 paperclips long'. The rule is that every unit must be the **same size**, and they must line up end to end with no gaps.

The trouble with paperclips and hand-spans is that everyone's are different, so we'd all get different answers. That's why we have **standard units** that never change — like **centimetres** and **metres** for length, **grams** and **kilograms** for weight, and **litres** for how much a container holds.

example.problem: A book is measured as 6 paperclips long. What must be true about the paperclips?
steps: Units used to measure must all be the same size.
They must be placed end to end with no gaps and no overlaps.
So all 6 paperclips must be identical and lined up neatly.
example.answer: All the paperclips must be the same size, lined up end to end.

sections.heading: The right tool and the right unit
body: Different things need different tools. We use a **ruler** or tape for length, a **balance or scales** for weight, and a **measuring cup or jug** for capacity. We also pick a unit that fits: you'd measure a pencil in centimetres but a room in metres, because using tiny units for big things means counting forever.
Measuring well is a real-life skill — cooking, building, and shopping all need it — and it all starts with comparing and counting equal units.

practice.q: To compare two pencils fairly for length, you should:
options: Line them up at the same starting point
practice.explain: Line them up at the same start and see which sticks out further — that tells you which is longer.

practice.q: When you measure with units like paperclips, the units must be:
practice.explain: Units must all be the same size and placed end to end with no gaps, or the count won't be fair.

practice.q: Why do we use standard units like centimetres instead of hand-spans?
options: Everyone's hand-span is different, so answers wouldn't match
practice.explain: Standard units never change, so everyone measuring gets the same answer.

practice.q: Which tool would you use to measure how heavy something is?
practice.explain: Weight is measured with a balance or scales; a ruler is for length and a jug for capacity.

practice.q: Which unit best fits measuring the length of a room?
practice.explain: A room is large, so metres fit; centimetres would take a very long time to count.

summary: Compare first: longer/shorter for length, heavier/lighter for weight, holds more/less for capacity.
To measure how much, count equal-sized units placed end to end with no gaps.
Standard units (cm, m, grams, kg, litres) never change, so everyone gets the same answer.
Use the right tool and a unit that fits the size of the thing.
